fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Infection - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Postpartum infections represent a critical yet often underrecognized threat to maternal health, contributing significantly to global morbidity and mortality. Affecting 5% to 7% of postpartum patients, these infections account for up to 15% of deaths following delivery and rank among the top causes of peripartum mortality in both low- and high-resource settings. Delays in recognition and management contribute to poor outcomes, with a majority of sepsis-related deaths considered preventable. This activity provides clinicians with an in-depth review of the clinical presentation, evaluation, and treatment of postpartum infections, including endomyometritis, septic abortion, surgical site infections, necrotizing fasciitis, and septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Evidence-based strategies to improve timely diagnosis, apply effective empiric and targeted antimicrobial therapy, and recognize when surgical intervention is indicated are also reviewed. This course also covers postpartum infection risk factors, infection prevention strategies across the continuum of care, as well as clinical decision-making in both resource-rich and resource-limited settings, and individualized care considerations for breastfeeding patients. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying postpartum infections, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition, improving clinical vigilance and adherence to current best practices to reduce preventable maternal harm and enhance outcomes in the postpartum period. Objectives: * Identify the various etiologies of postpartum infections. * Determine the appropriate steps for the evaluation of postpartum infections. * Create management options for the various postpartum infections. * Strategize with interprofessional teams to improve care coordination in the treatment of postpartum infections to improve overall patient outcomes. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Pregnancy-related morbidity and mortality are global socioeconomic and healthcare burdens, and postpartum infections account for a significant and often preventable portion of that burden. The postpartum period is traditionally defined as the 6 weeks following delivery, and infections are relatively common, affecting an estimated 5% to 7% of patients during this time. Puerperal sepsis is one of the top 5 causes of pregnancy-related deaths worldwide and accounts for 10% to 15% of deaths in the postpartum period. In the United States, sepsis complicates 4 in 10,000 live births, but it is the second leading cause of peripartum death. Rates of postpartum sepsis continue to increase.[1] In over 60% of these cases, delays in recognition or management occur, and an estimated 63% of parental deaths from sepsis may have been prevented.[2][3][2] Infections are also the most common cause of death following spontaneous or induced abortions. The medical burden of these infections is compounded by the alarmingly rapid increase in bacterial resistance to commonly used antibiotics.[4] Postpartum infections also present a significant social burden as they increase parental anxiety, the risk of postpartum depression, interfere with bonding, and can negatively impact breastfeeding.[5][6] Postpartum infections discussed in this course include infections that occur after live births, stillbirths, and spontaneous or induced abortions. Mastitis is not included in this discussion, as it does not directly result from pregnancy or delivery. Etiology Most postpartum infections arise from physiologic or iatrogenic trauma to the abdominal wall and the reproductive, genital, or urinary tract during childbirth or abortion. This trauma can disrupt normal barriers and facilitate the spread of bacteria into deeper tissues or sites where infection can develop. Epidemiology Studying rates of postpartum infections and their effects is difficult, as most of these infections occur following hospital discharge. Trends toward decreasing hospital stay following childbirth further inhibit the detection of postpartum complications, including infection.[7] Available data shows that postpartum infections account for 19% of birthing persons' deaths following stillbirth and 34% following spontaneous or induced abortions.[8] The latest data from the Centers for Disease Control show that infections disproportionately affect ethnic minorities and are the leading cause of pregnancy-related deaths among Hispanic people in the United States.[9] On the whole, postpartum infections are more common in patients who underwent cesarean section as opposed to vaginal delivery, and the risk is further increased for patients who underwent labor before the cesarean section.[10] Approximately 1% to 3% of patients with uncomplicated vaginal deliveries will be diagnosed with postpartum endometritis.[11] The risk of postpartum infections is likewise increased in patients at the extremes of age or with high body mass index, diabetes, hypertension, or immune compromise. As the BMI increases, the risk of postcesarean wound infection also increases.[12] Patients with bacterial vaginosis or sexually transmitted infections, as well as group-B streptococcus (GBS) carriers, also have an increased risk of postpartum infections.[13] Birth events associated with increased risk of infection include preterm or post-term labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, HIV infection, thick meconium stained amniotic fluid, operative vaginal delivery, retained products of conception, use of a foley catheter, uterine cleaning at cesarean section, manual removal of the placenta, uterine instrumentation, and postpartum hemorrhage.[14][11] Frequent vaginal exams in labor and internal fetal or uterine monitoring may also increase the risk, although this has been debated.[13…

fetched_contents.text: Endometritis - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Endometritis is an infectious inflammation of the endometrium that can cause severe long-term complications in women if not correctly diagnosed and treated. Diagnosing endometritis can be difficult and is frequently underdiagnosed due to its wide range of potential clinical features. Management requires accurate and prompt recognition of the conditions, appropriate antibiotics, and coordination between interdisciplinary professionals. This educational activity addresses various aspects of endometritis, including its classification into acute and chronic forms. It explores the clinical manifestations, diagnostic challenges, and implications, shedding light on the differences between endometritis and pelvic inflammatory disease. The activity emphasizes the vital role of the healthcare team in evaluating, diagnosing, and managing patients with endometritis, addressing both symptomatic presentations and asymptomatic cases that may contribute to conditions like recurrent pregnancy loss and infertility. Objectives: * Identify the clinical manifestations and risk factors associated with endometriosis, such as dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and infertility. * Utilize appropriate diagnostic tools and assessments to screen for endometriosis in symptomatic patients. * Tailor treatment strategies to individual patient needs, considering factors like symptom severity, desire for fertility, and comorbid conditions. * Coordinate care and follow-up to ensure seamless coordination of care, referrals, and long-term follow-up to optimize patient outcomes and quality of life. Introduction Endometritis is inflammation localized to the endometrium, the inner uterine lining, commonly due to an infectious etiology.[1] Infection that extends to the fallopian tubes, ovaries, or pelvic peritoneum is termed pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).[2] Endometritis is traditionally classified into 2 types: acute and chronic. Postpartum endometritis is a subtype of acute endometritis associated with pregnancy.[3][4] Acute endometritis unrelated to pregnancy refers to an endometrial infection present for ≤30 days.[3] It is typically due to a sexually transmitted infection (STI) or bacterial vaginosis (BV). Common symptoms are similar to those of PID (eg, fever, pelvic pain, vaginal discharge) and can range from mild to severe. Because of the overlapping symptoms, some clinicians consider acute endometritis to be synonymous with PID.[2][3][2] Histologically, it is characterized by the formation of microabscesses and neutrophilic invasion into the endometrium.[5] Additionally, although acute salpingitis, which frequently accompanies acute endometritis in PID, is associated with tubal factor infertility due to scarring, acute endometritis alone is not associated with reduced fertility rates.[5][6] Chronic endometritis is mild inflammation of the endometrium, typically due to microbial colonization not associated with pregnancy that lasts ≥30 days.[3] It is characterized by plasma cells in the endometrial stroma and other signs of chronic inflammation. Patients are often asymptomatic; however, the most common presenting symptoms are abnormal uterine bleeding, dyspareunia, and pelvic pain. Chronic endometritis is also frequently cited as contributing to recurrent pregnancy loss and infertility. The condition can be difficult to diagnose because, unlike acute endometritis, no defined diagnostic parameters other than endometrial stromal plasmacytes are considered sensitive histologic findings in most studies.[5][7][8] Postpartum endometritis is the most common cause of postpartum infection. Most cases of postpartum endometritis are polymicrobial, involving aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, and are due to the translocation of normal vaginal flora into the uterine cavity during labor and delivery.[4] Endometritis is 5 to 20 times more common in patients undergoing cesarean delivery than vaginal delivery.[4] Etiology Endometritis primarily results from the ascension of microorganisms from the lower genital tract (ie, the cervix and vaginal vault) into the endometrial cavity. The specific pathogens more frequently found to infect the endometrium vary depending on the type of endometritis and are sometimes difficult to identify.[3][4] Acute Endometritis In acute endometritis, >85% of infectious etiologies are caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Unlike chronic and postpartum endometritis, which have multiple organisms linked to causation, the primary microbial etiology of acute endometritis is Chlamydia trachomatis, followed by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and BV-associated bacteria.[3][6] Risk factors for acute endometritis include age <25 years, a history of STIs, engaging in high-risk sexual behavior such as having multiple partners, and undergoing gynecologic procedures like placing intrauterine devices or endometrial biopsies. These factors contribute to the increased susceptibility to this condition among certain individuals.[9][5][6] Chronic Endometritis The etiology of chronic endometritis is often unknown. Some studies have shown possible endometrial inflammation associated with noninfectious etiologies (eg, intrauterine contraceptive devices, endometrial polyps, submucosal leiomyomas).[10] However, when a causative organism is identified, it is frequently a polymicrobial infection comprised of microorganisms commonly found in the vaginal vault. fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Hemorrhage: Overview, Etiology, Diagnosis Although most postpartum hemorrhages can be controlled by medical management, a surgical approach can be lifesaving when pharmacologic and other nonsurgical strategies fail. The initial procedure of choice is often dictated by the cause of PPH, the route of delivery, and the timing of PPH. To reduce the risk of severe morbidity and mortality, the decision to move to a surgical method should be made swiftly when more conservative measures are unsuccessful. Here we will discuss surgical options from the least to the most invasive. Minimally invasive techniques are as follows: * Laceration repair * Uterine evacuation * Vascular embolization and occlusion Techniques at the time of laparotomy are as follows: * Uterine compression * Vascular ligation * Hysterectomy Minimally invasive techniques Laceration repair Genital tract trauma is the most likely cause if bleeding is persistent or is present despite a well-contracted uterus. Genital tract laceration leading to hemorrhage primarily requires procedural management for resolution. The vulva, vagina, and cervix are the most common anatomic sites of laceration that necessitates transvaginal repair. Multiple strategies for suture repair can be effective. A running, locked technique is often employed using an absorbable suture such as polyglycolic acid. Incorporation of the laceration apex is imperative. Expeditious repair can be aided with adequate exposure to the laceration including optimal lighting, positioning, and utilization of vaginal retractors. Adequate anesthesia is also necessary, and repair in the operating room should be considered. Additionally, consideration can be made for 24 hours of vaginal packing following laceration repair if continued venous oozing is identified. Extensive genital tract injury involving adjacent structures, such as the uterus, bladder, rectum, and retroperitoneum, leading to hemorrhage is rare. Lacerations high in the vaginal vault and those extending up from the cervix may involve the uterus or lead to broad ligament or retroperitoneal hematomas. The proximity of the ureters to the lateral vaginal fornices, and the base of the bladder to the anterior fornix, must be kept in mind when repair is undertaken in these areas. Poorly placed stitches can lead to genitourinary fistulas. Additional techniques may be required in these circumstances, and a laparotomy may be necessary. Expanding lower genital tract hematomas may be managed by incision and drainage when interventional vascular specialists are unavailable or interventional approaches are otherwise contraindicated. Surgically, any bleeding vessels are ligated, oozing areas may be oversewn, and the surgical bed is packed. It is recommended to place a Foley catheter to avoid urinary retention secondary to pain and tissue distortion. Uterine evacuation Uterine evacuation is effective at managing hemorrhage associated with uterine atony and retained products of conception such as the placenta. The usual approach is via a suction curettage, although manual removal and sharp curettage may also be utilized. For suction curettage, an electric suction or manual vacuum aspirator can be used transvaginally. These devices create a negative pressure system to aid in clearing the uterine contents. The size of the cannula is chosen based on an estimated volume of uterine contents to be evacuated and dilation of the cervix. Efficient evacuation lessens additional hemorrhage. See the Medscape article Dilation and Curettage With Suction for more details. Manual removal of products of conception or clot burden can also be utilized. These strategies may be used transvaginally or intraoperatively during a cesarean delivery. When manual removal of the placenta is required, care should be taken to identify a distinct plane along the uteroplacental margin. A high index of suspicion should be maintained for the possibility of a morbidly adherent placenta, which would necessitate more extensive treatment. Each evacuation technique requires adequate anesthesia, and antiseptic techniques are recommended. The routine use of a single dose of antibiotics is advised. Some clinicians utilize ultrasound guidance, although ultrasonography has not been shown to consistently reduce complication rates in this setting. Vascular embolization and occlusion Pelvic vascular embolization is a highly successful, minimally invasive approach to control postpartum hemorrhage. Selective arterial embolization may be useful in situations in which preservation of fertility is desired, when surgical options have been exhausted, and in managing hematomas.The procedure utilizes diagnostic angiography followed by introduction of an agent to occlude the selected arteries. The preferred agents are dissolvable and temporary, although permanent substances are also available. The success rate of uterine artery embolization following PPH has been reported as higher than 90%. [3, 13] Access to this technique may be limited by the availability of personnel and equipment; thus, early communication with an interventional specialist is warranted. Although not an absolute contraindication, patients are preferably hemodynamically stable and noncoagulopathic prior to embolization. Active monitoring of the patient’s clinical status should continue throughout the procedure. Vascular occlusion balloons can also be placed by an interventional vascular specialist. These balloons can be placed within the hypogastric and common iliac arteries, and even the aorta. They are then later inflated to temporarily occlude the pelvic vasculature, minimizing hemorrhage. This technique is most frequently used prophylactically in surgical cases of high suspicion for massive hemorrhage. Branch report on likely urgent postpartum complications and deterioration risk

Postpartum complications that can worsen quickly are those that can rapidly progress to sepsis, shock, or death if not treated promptly. The evidence clearly states that postpartum infections can progress to sepsis, bacteremia, shock, and death if not treated appropriately, and that necrotizing fasciitis is especially known for this rapid progression [N1-R1]. Similarly, postpartum hemorrhage is described as a medical emergency that remains one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide, with surgical options needed when medical management fails [N4-F3]. The postpartum period is also noted to be a time when infections can be missed because many complications occur after hospital discharge, and the risk of maternal sepsis continues after childbirth [N1-F2]. These factors make several postpartum conditions particularly worrisome because they can deteriorate rapidly and are often underrecognized until symptoms become severe [N1-F2].

The conditions most likely to worsen quickly include postpartum infection, particularly endometritis, and retained placenta or retained products of conception. Postpartum infection is highlighted as a major contributor to global maternal morbidity and mortality, with up to 15% of deaths following delivery attributed to it, and delays in recognition and management are a major contributor to poor outcomes [N1-F2]. The StatPearls material also lists postpartum uterine infections, prolonged labor, retained placenta, and other birth-related trauma as common sources of infection [N1-R2]. Retained placenta is especially dangerous because undiagnosed retained placenta can result in significant hemorrhage, maternal morbidity, and even mortality [N1-R5]. Endometritis, a common postpartum infection, can also progress to sepsis, toxic shock, and necrotizing fasciitis, which explains why it is considered a red flag [N6-R1].

Clinical features that may suggest infection or other acute issues are not limited to fever. The evidence points to several red flags: pronounced suprapubic and uterine tenderness, enlarged postpartum uterine size, and alarm findings such as those associated with sepsis [N2-R1]. The endometritis source also lists pain, diarrhea, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge as features that may accompany infection, and it emphasizes that diagnosis is clinical and rarely aided by endometrial culture [N6-R1]. Another source notes that common symptoms of postpartum endometritis include fever, pelvic pain, and vaginal discharge, but the evidence also indicates that fever is not always present early, and that alarm findings are important for identifying patients at risk for sepsis [N2-R4]. Therefore, even in the absence of fever, a patient with lower abdominal tenderness, uterine tenderness, or foul-smelling lochia should be taken seriously [N1-R4; N2-R1].

What is most important if deterioration happens is prompt recognition and treatment. The StatPearls material emphasizes prompt recognition and treatment as critical to prevent severe complications [N1-R1]. For postpartum hemorrhage, early communication with an interventional specialist is warranted because pelvic vascular embolization can be lifesaving when surgical options are exhausted or when preservation of fertility is desired [N4-F3]. For postpartum infection, the evidence supports rapid evaluation, appropriate empiric and targeted antimicrobial therapy, and surgical intervention when indicated [N1-F2]. The same source also highlights that delays in recognition or management contribute to poor outcomes and that most sepsis-related deaths may be preventable [N1-F2]. In short, immediate actions should focus on rapid evaluation, administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics when infection is suspected, and surgical or interventional consultation for complications such as retained placenta or hemorrhage [N1-F2; N4-F3].

Branch report on infection risk and whether feverless symptoms may still be concerning

Risk factors that increase postpartum infection likelihood are clearly identified in the evidence. The StatPearls source lists several risk factors: cesarean section versus vaginal delivery, prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, retained products of conception, manual removal of the placenta, uterine instrumentation, postpartum hemorrhage, and the use of a Foley catheter [N1-F2]. It also notes that postpartum infections are more common in patients with high body mass index, diabetes, hypertension, immune compromise, and in those with bacterial vaginosis or STIs, as well as GBS carriers [N1-F2]. Obstetric risk factors specifically include preterm or post-term labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labor, HIV infection, thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid, operative vaginal delivery, retained products of conception, use of a Foley catheter, uterine cleaning at cesarean section, manual removal of the placenta, uterine instrumentation, and postpartum hemorrhage [N1-F2]. Endometritis-specific risk factors include maternal obesity, diabetes, tobacco use, immunosuppression, and obstetric risk factors such as those listed above [N2-R3]. These risk factors matter because they increase the likelihood of infection and complicate the clinical picture, making early recognition more difficult [N1-F2; N2-R3].

Non-fever signs that may still signal infection or other complications are important because fever is not always the first or only sign. The evidence shows that postpartum infection can present with fever above 38°C, chills, weakness, lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and fast breathing, but it also emphasizes that fever is not always present early, and that alarm findings are important for identifying patients at risk for sepsis [N1-R4; N2-R4]. Endometritis is described as an infectious inflammation of the endometrium that can cause severe long-term complications if not diagnosed and treated, and its clinical manifestations are wide-ranging and often underdiagnosed [N2-F1]. The endometritis source also states that common symptoms are similar to those of PID, including fever, pelvic pain, and vaginal discharge, but it also notes that diagnosis is clinical and rarely aided by endometrial culture [N2-R1; N2-R2]. This means that feverless symptoms such as lower abdominal tenderness, uterine tenderness, abnormal uterine size, or foul-smelling lochia can still be concerning and should not be dismissed [N2-R1; N1-R4].

Mild lower abdominal tenderness in this context is best interpreted as a red flag rather than a benign finding. The evidence states that clinical findings of postpartum endometritis include pronounced suprapubic and uterine tenderness, enlarged postpartum uterine size, and alarm findings [N2-R1]. It also notes that postpartum endometritis may progress to sepsis, toxic shock, and necrotizing fasciitis, and that it is one of the most common causes of postpartum infection [N6-R1; N6-R2]. In addition, retained placenta is highlighted as a condition that can result in significant hemorrhage and maternal morbidity/mortality, with retained products of conception being a risk factor for infection [N1-R2; N1-R5]. Because mild tenderness may be early or mild, it should not be ignored, especially in someone with risk factors, a recent delivery, or any other signs of infection or hemorrhage [N1-F2; N2-R1; N2-R3]. In short, mild lower abdominal tenderness may be a sign of infection, endometritis, retained products, or other acute postpartum complications, and should be evaluated carefully rather than assumed to be harmless [N2-R1; N6-R1].

Branch report on diagnostic and management decision-making in a low-fever setting

Diagnostic testing is reasonable without fever when there is a clinical suspicion of infection or other acute postpartum complications. The evidence supports a clinical diagnosis for postpartum endometritis, which is described as being primarily clinical and rarely aided by endometrial culture [N2-R1; N2-R2]. It also states that signs and symptoms are important for identifying alarm findings and patients at risk for sepsis [N2-R4]. For sepsis and infection, the StatPearls source emphasizes that delays in recognition and management contribute to poor outcomes, and that evidence-based strategies include timely diagnosis and appropriate empiric and targeted antimicrobial therapy [N1-F2]. This suggests that diagnostic testing should not be limited to fever; rather, it should be guided by clinical suspicion, especially when the patient has risk factors, retained products, prolonged labor, or other obstetric risk factors [N1-F2; N2-R3].

Lab results would change interpretation when fever is absent because infection and sepsis can still be present without fever. The evidence explicitly notes that alarm findings are important for identifying patients at risk for sepsis, and that diagnosis is clinical rather than solely dependent on fever [N2-R4]. It also states that postpartum infections can progress to sepsis, bacteremia, shock, and death if not treated appropriately [N1-R1]. This means that normal or mild lab results should not rule out infection, especially in someone with risk factors, retained placenta, or other acute symptoms [N1-F2; N2-R4]. The management guidance in the StatPearls source also emphasizes that delays in recognition or management contribute to poor outcomes, and that most sepsis-related deaths may be preventable [N1-F2]. Therefore, lab results should be interpreted alongside clinical features rather than as standalone evidence, because feverless postpartum symptoms can still be concerning [N2-R4; N1-F2].

A specialist or emergency evaluation is most needed when there is evidence of rapid progression, alarm findings, or a high suspicion of sepsis, retained products, or hemorrhage. The evidence shows that postpartum infection can rapidly progress to sepsis, bacteremia, shock, and death if not treated appropriately [N1-R1]. For postpartum hemorrhage, the material states that surgical options may be lifesaving when pharmacologic and other nonsurgical strategies fail, and that early communication with an interventional specialist is warranted [N4-F3]. The StatPearls source also states that delays in recognition or management contribute to poor outcomes and that most sepsis-related deaths may be preventable [N1-F2]. In a low-fever setting, a specialist evaluation is especially important if the patient has persistent or worsening lower abdominal tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, fever or alarm findings, retained products, or any signs of sepsis [N1-R4; N2-R4; N1-F2]. In short, low fever does not mean low risk; specialist or emergency evaluation is most needed when clinical suspicion is high and the patient is not improving, because the consequences of delay can be severe [N1-F2; N4-F3; N2-R4].

Branch report on follow-up guidance and practical next steps

How soon the patient should seek care if symptoms change depends on the degree of concern and the presence of alarm findings. The evidence indicates that severe abdominal pain 5 days after vaginal delivery is unusual and should immediately prompt evaluation for unrecognized complications [N3-R4]. It also states that in more severe situations, the patient may have fever, chills, lower abdominal pain, or uterine tenderness, anorexia, lethargy, and rapid pulse, and that treatment should be initiated promptly [N3-R3]. For the patient described here, the key message is that any worsening of mild lower abdominal tenderness, fever, chills, or other symptoms should not be ignored; care should be sought sooner rather than later if symptoms change [N3-R3; N3-R4]. In other words, the patient should seek care within hours to days if symptoms get worse, especially if they develop fever, worsening pain, or signs of sepsis.

What to watch for before going to the ER or clinic includes symptoms that signal rapid deterioration. The most important red flags are fever, chills, lower abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, anorexia, lethargy, and rapid pulse [N3-R3]. The evidence also highlights that postpartum infection can progress to sepsis, bacteremia, shock, and death if not treated appropriately, and that prompt recognition and treatment are critical to prevent severe complications [N1-R1; N1-F2]. In addition, retained products of conception and postpartum hemorrhage can rapidly worsen, requiring urgent evaluation and intervention [N1-R2; N4-F3]. So the patient should watch for any new or worsening fever, increasing pain, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, weakness, or signs of dehydration or shock, and should go to the ER or clinic immediately if these appear [N1-R4; N3-R3].

Whether telehealth or urgent care is appropriate depends on the urgency of the situation. The upstream infection-risk branch indicates that feverless symptoms can still be concerning and that diagnostic testing may be reasonable without fever if there is clinical suspicion of infection [N8]. In that context, telehealth may be acceptable for a low-risk patient with mild symptoms and no rapid deterioration, but urgent care is more appropriate if there is any doubt about infection, retained products, or hemodynamic instability [N8; N1-F2]. The postpartum care guidance also emphasizes that an office visit is recommended within the first 7 days after delivery and that ongoing care should be provided as needed [N3-R1]. However, because the patient has delayed follow-up and mild lower abdominal tenderness, urgent care is likely more appropriate than relying solely on telehealth, especially if symptoms are not clearly benign [N3-R1; N3-R4]. In short, telehealth can be used cautiously for mild concerns, but urgent care should be used if symptoms change or if the patient feels unwell enough to warrant immediate in-person evaluation [N3-R1; N3-R4].

- If symptoms are only slightly worse, but you are still concerned, go to **urgent care** rather than waiting for a routine follow-up [N3-R4; N3-R1].

### B) Watch for these alarm signs before going to the ER or clinic
- **Fever above 38°C**
- **Chills**
- **Worsening lower abdominal pain**
- **Uterine tenderness**
- **Foul-smelling vaginal discharge or lochia**
- **Weakness, lethargy, or anorexia**
- **Rapid pulse or signs of dehydration** [N1-R4; N3-R3]

### C) Consider telehealth only cautiously
- Telehealth can be used if symptoms are **mild and stable**, but it is **not a substitute for urgent evaluation if there is any doubt** [N3-R1; N8].
- If you are unsure, it is better to go to **urgent care** or the **ER** rather than relying only on telehealth [N8; N1-F2].

### D) What a provider may do
- A provider may ask about symptoms, fever, and other signs of infection or sepsis.
- They may perform a physical exam, including **uterine and suprapubic tenderness**.
- They may order **labs** if there is concern for infection, and may consider **imaging** if retained products or hemorrhage is suspected [N1-F2; N2-R4].
- They may prescribe **antibiotics** if infection is suspected, and may refer you to **surgery or interventional care** if needed [N4-F3; N1-F2].

## 9) Bottom line for you

Your situation is **not normal**, but it is **not automatically a life-threatening emergency** either. **Mild lower abdominal tenderness after childbirth, especially with a slight suspicion of infection, is concerning enough to warrant prompt follow-up**, especially if you have not yet followed up [N2-R1; N3-R4]. The evidence shows that postpartum infections can progress quickly to sepsis, and that retained products or hemorrhage can also worsen rapidly [N1-R1; N4-F3].

### What you should do:
- **Do not ignore the symptoms**.
- **Seek care sooner if symptoms change**.
- **Go to the ER or clinic immediately if you develop fever, worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge, weakness, or other alarm signs** [N1-R4; N3-R3].
- **Use urgent care rather than relying only on telehealth if you are concerned** [N3-R1; N8].

If you are unsure, the safest choice is to **go to urgent care or the ER** rather than waiting for a routine follow-up [N3-R4; N8].
